analysis.one_liner: Requires smart devices with microphones to disclose and let users turn off ambient-audio collection.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require makers of internet-connected devices with microphones — smart speakers, smart TVs, connected appliances — to tell buyers up front how the device collects sound from the room, including human conversation, and whether that information is kept, shared with third parties, or used for targeted advertising. Manufacturers would have to provide a simple switch to turn that collection off and back on, could share the collected information only under narrow legal or safety circumstances with notice to the user, and could not keep it longer than needed. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, though companies could satisfy the bill instead by following industry-written self-regulatory guidelines approved by the FTC.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who owns or lives around internet-connected devices with microphones: smart speakers, smart TVs, connected doorbells, appliances, and toys. The bill would give them plain-language notice that the device may be listening to ambient sound in their home, disclosure of how long recordings are kept and whether they are sold or used for ad targeting, and an easy way to switch the collection off. It would also let state attorneys general sue manufacturers on residents' behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of smart speakers and connected devices

how_it_helps.text: Requires a clear, plain-language notice at first power-on — in audio and text — describing how the device collects ambient noise, how long the manufacturer keeps it, and whether it is disclosed to third parties or used for targeted advertising.
Requires a 'reasonable and easy' mechanism for the device owner to deactivate and reactivate the collection of covered information.

Restricts manufacturer disclosures of collected information to legal process and urgent-safety circumstances, and requires the manufacturer to notify the affected user within 7 days of any disclosure, naming the third party that received it.
Bars manufacturers from retaining collected information longer than reasonably necessary for the stated purpose.
Enforcement is available to the FTC and to state attorneys general, who may obtain civil penalties, restitution, and compensation for residents.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of internet-connected devices with microphones would bear the cost of providing notices, building a deactivate mechanism, tracking and limiting retention, and notifying users of any disclosures — and would lose the ability to freely share ambient-audio data with advertisers and data brokers. Ad-tech and data-broker firms would lose a source of in-home audio-derived data. Consumers could see slightly higher device prices or fewer always-on listening features.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains a safe harbor: a manufacturer is 'deemed to be in compliance' if it follows self-regulatory guidelines written by representatives of the marketing or covered-devices industries and approved by the FTC, letting the industry write the rules it must follow.
The bill does not take effect until the FTC approves a set of self-regulatory guidelines — up to 2 years after enactment if the FTC never approves any — so real-world protection would be delayed.
The bill contains no private right of action, so individual consumers could not sue on their own; enforcement would rest entirely on the FTC and state attorneys general.

It excludes wake-word-activated collection — the core mode of smart speakers — from the definition of 'ambient noise,' so the routine voice commands devices capture are not covered; only always-on listening outside of user activation is.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protection is real but modest: it would make always-on listening visible and switchable and restrict data sharing, at a compliance cost to device makers. Its weaknesses — the industry safe harbor, a delay of up to two years before any part takes effect, no private right of action, and exclusion of wake-word collection — leave the strongest practices largely untouched, so even if enacted it would be a floor rather than a fix. As introduced, it never got far enough for any of this to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Scalise introduced the bill on July 27, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress, and no member signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on July 27, 2022; the action history shows no further activity of any kind.
The bill never received a committee hearing or markup, never reached the House floor, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of internet-connected devices with microphones and the data brokers and ad-tech firms that buy ambient-audio-derived information, who continue collecting and sharing in-home audio data with no federal notice, opt-out, or retention limits. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Steve Scalise
for.role: House Majority Whip (117th Congress); introduced the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the EAVESDROP Act in the House on July 27, 2022.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 27, 2022 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the remaining five-plus months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member of either party supported the bill — a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party — so no partisan pattern ever developed; the bill simply had no visible support base.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of internet-connected devices with microphones (smart speakers, smart TVs, connected appliances, wearables)
industries.note: These companies profit from devices that listen in homes; the bill would force them to disclose ambient-audio collection, build an off switch, limit retention, and notify users of disclosures, cutting into the data and feature pipeline their products are built around. A safe harbor letting the industry write its own FTC-approved guidelines, and a wake-word exclusion, soften the burden.

The bill restricts manufacturers to selling or sharing ambient-audio-derived data only for legal process or urgent safety, with notice to users, sharply limiting the third-party market for in-home voice data. Explicitly excludes data brokers from 'service provider' status, so they could not be used as a workaround.
Manufacturers must disclose whether they process collected information for targeted advertising and face limits on sharing it, reducing the availability of ambient-audio signals for ad targeting.
